opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so Glaze really came out of conversations we had with artists back in late 2022. What we heard over and over was this sense of real distress: people were watching others take twenty or thirty of their images, fine-tune a model on them, and suddenly produce work "in the style of" that artist, sometimes even selling it or posting it under their name. For a lot of independent artists, their style is their livelihood. It's what gets them commissions, what makes them recognizable. So the mimicry is a real economic and personal harm, not just a hypothetical.

What Glaze does is fairly simple to describe at a high level. Before an artist posts their work online, they run it through Glaze, which computes a set of very small perturbations to the image. To a human eye, the artwork looks essentially the same. But to the feature extractors these generative models use, the image appears to sit in a very different place in style space. So if someone scrapes those images and tries to fine-tune a model to mimic that artist, what the model learns is a shifted, distorted version of the style rather than the artist's actual style.

I want to be clear about what Glaze is and isn't. It's not a permanent, bulletproof solution. This is an adversarial space, and we've always said that. There will be attempts to get around these protections, and we keep updating the tool in response. But I think of it as raising the cost of mimicry. Right now, the default is that anything an artist posts is free for the taking, with no consent and no compensation. Glaze gives artists some agency back, a way to say, "You can see my work, but you can't easily turn it into a model of me."

And honestly, part of the role is also signaling. When hundreds of thousands, and then millions, of downloads happen, it tells the industry and policymakers that artists really care about this and aren't okay with the status quo. Technology alone won't fix this. We need regulation, we need norms around consent. But in the meantime, artists need something they can use today, and that's the gap Glaze is trying to fill.

r001.rationale: The response says Glaze adds small perturbations that leave the artwork essentially unchanged to human viewers but make it appear very different in style space to models’ feature extractors.

r002.rationale: It explains that a model fine-tuned on treated images learns a shifted, distorted version of the artist’s style instead of the artist’s actual style.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. The way I think about Glaze is that it's a tool for individual artists, and that's a deliberate choice. When we started talking to artists in late 2022, right after Stable Diffusion came out, the thing that hurt them most wasn't some abstract concern about training data. It was that someone could type their name into a prompt, or grab twenty of their images, fine-tune a model for a few hours, and produce work that looked convincingly like theirs. That's a very personal kind of harm. It's your name, your reputation, your livelihood, and it's happening at the level of a single person who has no leverage against a company or a random Discord user.

So Glaze operates on the artist's own images before they post them. It computes a small perturbation, something that's barely visible to a human, that shifts how the image is represented inside the feature space these models use. The human sees your watercolor. The model sees something closer to, say, Van Gogh or a cubist style. If someone then tries to fine-tune on those Glazed images to mimic you, what they get back doesn't look like your work. The mimicry fails, or at least degrades enough that it's not useful.

I want to be honest about what that is and isn't. It's not a silver bullet. It's a defense in an adversarial setting, which means it's part of an arms race, and we've been upfront that it will need updates as models and attacks change. It also doesn't retroactively protect the millions of images already scraped. What it does is give artists a way to keep sharing their work publicly, which they need to do to get commissions and build a career, without handing over a clean training set to anyone who wants to clone them.

The other role, which I think is maybe underappreciated, is that it changes the economics a bit. If mimicry gets harder and less reliable, the people doing it have less incentive, and it buys time for the legal and policy side to catch up. We've always said the real long-term solution has to involve regulation, licensing, consent. Glaze is what artists can do today, on their own, while that plays out. And the fact that millions of people have downloaded it tells you how badly they wanted something, anything, that put some control back in their hands.

r001.rationale: It says the perturbation is barely visible to people, while the model perceives the image as closer to another style, such as Van Gogh or cubism.

r002.rationale: It explains that fine-tuning on Glazed images produces work that no longer looks like the artist’s work, conveying that training shifts the learned style away from the intended target.

astra-6.text:
I see Glaze as a way to give artists some control over how their work is used. An artist may want to share their work online, reach an audience, and build a career without also making it easy for someone to train a model to imitate their style.

The idea is to make subtle changes to an image that leave it looking largely the same to a human viewer, but change how a model interprets its style. If someone uses those protected images for training, the goal is for the model to learn something different from the style the artist is trying to protect.

It’s not a complete solution, and I wouldn’t frame it as a permanent guarantee. But it can provide a practical layer of protection while the broader questions around consent and compensation are worked out. Ultimately, we want artists to have a meaningful choice about whether their work helps train these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says Glaze makes subtle image changes that leave the work looking largely the same to people while changing how a model interprets its style.

r002.rationale: It explains that training on protected images is intended to make the model learn something different from the artist’s style.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of Glaze as a way to give artists some agency over how their work is used. There’s a difference between putting your art online so people can enjoy it and agreeing to have that art used to train a model that can imitate you.

The goal is to let artists continue sharing their work while making it harder for a model to learn their individual style. It’s a defensive tool, and I wouldn’t frame it as a permanent solution to the whole problem. But it can provide protection while we work through the broader questions of consent and how artists should be treated in this ecosystem.

r001.rationale: The response says Glaze makes it harder for models to learn an artist’s style, but does not explain that it alters artwork so human-perceived style stays largely unchanged while AI-perceived style substantially diverges.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that training on Glaze-treated artwork leads a model to learn a different style from the artist’s intended target style.
